title: Ashvala asks about death and ritual (3.1)
hook: the king's own hotri priest asks how a ritual can free anyone from death, and Yajnavalkya answers by turning each priest into a part of you
tomorrow: Artabhaga: "when a man dies, what does not leave him?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thousand cows with gold on their horns, and Yajnavalkya's answer: we bow to the wisest, we just want the cows. Your line was who is the wisest?

The first challenger is a professional. Ashvala is King Janaka's hotri, the priest whose job at the great fire sacrifice is to recite the hymns of the Rig Veda. He has spent his life inside the ritual: the right verse, the right moment, the right pitch. So he doesn't ask about the meaning of life. He asks about his own job. You think you're the wisest? Fine. Explain to me how what I do actually works.
screen: `THE FIRST CHALLENGER.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PRIEST.` → `EXPLAIN MY OWN JOB TO ME.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, Ashvala says, everything here is caught by death. By what does the one who offers the sacrifice get free of death? By the hotri priest, Yajnavalkya answers, by fire, by speech. Speech is the hotri of the sacrifice. Speech is this fire. That is freedom; that is freedom beyond. Ashvala tries again. Everything is caught by day and night. How does one get free of them? By the priest who handles the offerings, by the eye, by the sun. Everything is caught by the waxing and waning moon. By the priest who sings, by breath, by wind. And the sky has no stairs. How does the sacrificer climb to heaven? By the priest who oversees, by the mind, by the moon. See the pattern. Each of the four priests of the great sacrifice turns out to be a part of the person, speech, eye, breath, mind, and each of those a power of the cosmos, fire, sun, wind, moon. Yajnavalkya doesn't tell Ashvala the ritual is useless. He shows him what it's a picture of. The priest at the fire is also the voice in your throat. Then Ashvala asks a string of technical questions, how many verses, how many offerings, and Yajnavalkya answers each one. And Ashvala falls silent. Hindu thinkers have weighed this differently. The Mimamsa school held that the rites themselves are the heart of the Veda. Vedanta teachers read passages like this one as the rites pointing past themselves. Both kept the rites, and the fire rites are still performed today.
screen: `CAUGHT BY DEATH: HOW TO GET FREE?` · `THE PRIEST IS SPEECH; SPEECH IS FIRE.` · `FOUR PRIESTS, FOUR FACULTIES, FOUR POWERS.` · `ASHVALA FALLS SILENT.` · then, large: `FREEDOM, AND FREEDOM BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Notice speech first, even unspoken, the words forming in your mind, and let it be the fire. Then let your resting eyes be the sun, the breath coming and going the wind, and the mind watching all of it the moon. Nothing to perform: you're the whole ritual, sitting still.
Atimukti, freedom beyond. Ashvala's answer: the freedom the rite points to, when the priest is understood as speech, and speech as fire.
Your line: the priest who goes beyond. Tomorrow, a question about what stays when we die. See you then.

howItsDone: Vedic fire rituals, with their four kinds of priests, are still performed in parts of India; Hindu homes and temples keep smaller fire offerings, and Vedanta teachers read passages like this as showing the inner meaning of the rite.

what a scholar hears: hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman: the four priests mapped to speech/fire, eye/sun, breath/wind, mind/moon (3.1.3–6); sā muktiḥ sātimuktiḥ.

chat.says: So did Yajnavalkya tell the priest his rituals were pointless?
options: No, he showed what each rite pictures: the priest is speech, and speech is fire.
Yes, he told Ashvala the rites were useless and the fire should be put out.
No, but he admitted he didn't know what the four priests were for.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya showed each priest as a part of the person and a power of the cosmos: the hotri is speech, and speech is fire.
